title: Move a guitar's capo so that a singer's G chord shapes sound in A
instruction: The singer wants the next song in A, but she only knows how to play it with G chord shapes. Set the capo on her guitar for it.
context: Guitarists, accompanists, music teachers and guitar techs (O*NET 27-2042, 49-9063) move a capo so a song fits the singer's key without new chord shapes. A capo raises the strings one semitone per fret, so G shapes sound in A with the capo at the 2nd fret, counted from the nut. One fret off puts the whole song a semitone out of the singer's key.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left; heights above the table. Guitar, fixed (in a real trial its cradle and neck rest hold it): a full-size right-handed dreadnought steel-string acoustic, 650 mm scale, 104 cm long, in standard tuning, lying on its back, strings up, on a dark grey foam work mat 1 cm thick, its neck along y on the line x 30, resting in a beech neck rest with black felt cheeks under the 8th fret, headstock toward the robot's right (-y). Bone nut 43 mm across, its body-side face at y -27.0. Dark rosewood fretboard, level, its top 11.6 cm above the table, 43 mm wide at the nut and 45.4 mm at the 2nd fret wire. Twenty nickel-silver fret wires 2.7 mm wide and 1.2 mm tall; fret n's centre line is 650 x (1 - 2^(-n/12)) mm from the nut: 36.5, 70.9, 103.4, 134.1 and 163.1 mm for frets 1 to 5 (y -23.35, -19.91, -16.66, -13.59, -10.69). White pearloid dots 8 mm across in the 3rd, 5th, 7th, 9th, 15th and 17th fret spaces and two in the 12th; none in the 1st or 2nd. Six steel strings, four bronze-wound, low E farthest from the arms, 35 mm apart (1st to 6th, centre to centre) at the nut and 54 mm at the saddle, their tops 11.9 cm above the table. Black headstock face with three chrome tuners a side, tilted 14 degrees down, from the nut to y -45.5. Body from y +9.05 to +59.8, lower bout 39.7 cm, 10 cm deep: spruce top with soundhole, rosette and a black pickguard on the near side, mahogany sides and neck, rosewood bridge with a bone saddle at y +38.0. Capo, free to move (not fixed), about 47 g, in red anodised aluminium with black rubber pads: a cam-lever capo. Its C-shaped frame has a bar 66 mm long, 12 mm wide and 8 mm thick over a rubber pad 54 x 12 x 4 mm lying across the strings, and a spine 6 mm thick down the near side of the neck (toward the arms) to 48 mm below the pad, 7 mm clear of the neck's edge. A jaw (an aluminium bar 56 x 12 x 6 mm with a 3 mm rubber pad on top) runs under the neck from the spine and slides up and down it: clamped against the back of the neck with 25 N, or 10 mm below it when open. An aluminium rocker lever 8 mm wide sits on the bar, hinged 14 mm in from the spine: its handle runs 36 mm toward the far side and its tail 13 mm toward the spine, bent up 20 degrees. Closed (clamped), the handle lies flat on the bar and the tail stands 4 mm up; pressing the tail flat opens it, lifting the handle 20 degrees and dropping the jaw; pressing the handle flat closes it again. It starts clamped on the neck at the 4th fret, left from the previous song: square across the strings, lever closed, its bar's centre line in the middle of the 4th fret space (118.8 mm from the nut, y -15.12). Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: Read every control step from the capo's pose, its lever and jaw, and both grippers' TCPs (in a real trial: a photo from above, a side view, the video and a ruler). Distances are along the strings from the nut's body-side face; the 1st and 2nd fret wires' centre lines are at 36.5 and 70.9 mm. Crossing points: seen from above, where the centre line of the capo's 12 mm bar (and of the pad under it) crosses the 1st string (high E, nearest the arms) and the 6th string (low E). Clamped: the lever is closed, lying flat on the bar within 5 degrees; the capo is round the neck with the middle of the pad's underside within 2 mm of the string tops and the jaw within 2 mm of the neck's back; it is tilted less than 10 degrees from level. Square: seen from above, the bar is within 10 degrees of square to the strings. Released and still: both TCPs at least 6 cm from the middle of the pad's underside, and the capo has moved less than 1 mm in the last 1 s. Clean 2nd fret: both crossing points 44.0 to 63.4 mm from the nut (at least 7.5 mm from both wires' centre lines, so the bar covers neither wire). 2nd fret: both crossing points 44.0 to 78.4 mm from the nut (in the 2nd fret space or on top of the 2nd wire). 0 at any moment, for the rest of the trial: the capo moves more than 5 mm along the neck (at the middle of the pad's underside, from where it was when the lever last closed) while its lever is closed, lying flat on the bar within 5 degrees, whatever its tilt or height: a dragged capo, or the guitar moves more than 1 cm or turns more than 2 degrees (fixed in simulation, so only in a real trial). Otherwise: 1.0 once the capo is clamped, square, released, still and a clean 2nd fret for 1 s, which ends the trial. At the run limit, 0.5 if the capo is clamped, released, still and at the 2nd fret (on top of the 2nd wire, skewed more than 10 degrees, or a clean placement too late to hold 1 s). 0 in every other case, including the capo left at the 4th fret where it starts, at any other fret, on top of the 1st wire, at the 2nd fret but not clamped (lever open: it frets nothing, so the song stays in G), still held, closed on nothing, or off the neck. Possible scores: 0, 0.5, 1.0. Apart from the drag rule, the order of moves does not matter; the capo may be opened, moved and clamped again any number of times.
reset_notes: Clamp the capo back on the neck at the 4th fret: square, its bar in the middle of the 4th fret space, lever closed. Nothing is consumed.
fidelity: Rigid bodies at 240 Hz on GPU physics; the guitar is fixed. The capo is a three-link articulation (frame, sliding jaw, rocker lever). Its over-centre latch is logic and its 25 N clamp is a force-limited joint drive, so a press triggers the clamp but does not supply the force. The lever sits on the bar, not behind the neck. The strings are drawn and collide as one flat surface. No sound or pitch is simulated. Dots are 8 mm, not the usual 6.
